subtopics.title: Introduction to DataWeave
subtopics.meta_description: Learn what DataWeave 2.0 is, how it powers every data transformation in Mule 4, and how to write your first script inside the Transform Message component.
subtopics.summary: DataWeave 2.0 is Mule 4's native expression and transformation language used to read, reshape, and write data between formats.
subtopics.content_html:
DataWeave is the functional expression and transformation language built into every Mule 4 application. Wherever data needs to move from one shape to another — a JSON payload becoming XML, a CSV file becoming a Java object, or a simple variable assignment — DataWeave is the tool doing the work. Unlike Mule 3, where the Mule Expression Language (MEL) handled simple expressions and a separate DataWeave 1.0 engine handled transformations, Mule 4 unified everything under DataWeave 2.0. Every field in a Mule 4 flow that accepts a dynamic value — a variable assignment, a choice router condition, a connector parameter — can use DataWeave syntax.

Where DataWeave Runs

The most visible place you will write DataWeave is the Transform Message component, which appears in Anypoint Studio's Mule Palette as a dedicated processor. Behind the scenes, though, DataWeave also evaluates the content inside #[ ] expression markers used in almost every connector and scope, including <set-variable>, <logger>, and routing conditions in <choice>.

Anatomy of a DataWeave Script

Every .dwl script or Transform Message body is split into two parts: a header and a body, separated by three dashes (---). The header declares the DataWeave version and any input/output directives, imports, or variable declarations. The body is a single expression that produces the output.

%dw 2.0
input payload application/json
output application/json
---
{
  orderId: payload.id,
  customer: payload.customerName default "Unknown",
  total: payload.items map (item) -> item.price * item.quantity reduce ($, acc = 0) -> acc + $,
  itemCount: sizeOf(payload.items)
}

The %dw 2.0 line is mandatory and tells the runtime which language version to compile against. The output application/json directive tells DataWeave what MIME type to serialize the result to; you can freely swap it for application/xml, application/csv, application/java, and more. The body then constructs a new JSON object using selectors (payload.id), the default operator for null-safety, and higher-order functions like map and reduce.

Why DataWeave Replaced MEL

MEL in Mule 3 was adequate for simple expressions but could not express rich, nested transformations without dropping into Java or a separate DataWeave 1.0 file. DataWeave 2.0 closed that gap by becoming a full functional programming language with its own type system, pattern matching, modules, and a consistent syntax whether you are writing one line or two hundred.

AspectMEL (Mule 3)DataWeave 2.0 (Mule 4)
ScopeSimple expressions onlyExpressions and full transformations
Type systemJava-based, loosely typedRich native type system
Format supportLimited, needs extra transformersNative JSON, XML, CSV, Java, YAML, and more
ReusabilityNo module systemCustom modules and functions
Tip: You can prototype DataWeave scripts quickly in the DataWeave Playground inside Anypoint Studio (or the standalone online playground) before wiring them into a flow, which is especially useful when learning selector and function syntax.

Key Points

  • DataWeave 2.0 is the single expression and transformation language used throughout Mule 4.
  • Scripts have a header (version, directives, imports) and a body (the expression that produces output).
  • The Transform Message component is the primary UI for writing DataWeave, but expressions appear everywhere via #[ ].
  • DataWeave natively understands JSON, XML, CSV, Java, and other formats without extra converters.

subtopics.title: DataWeave Syntax and Selectors
subtopics.meta_description: Master DataWeave 2.0 selectors including single value, multi-value, index, range, and attribute selectors, with practical, real-world Mule 4 examples.
subtopics.summary: Selectors are how DataWeave scripts navigate into payloads to pull out the exact fields, attributes, or elements you need.
subtopics.content_html:
Once you can write a basic DataWeave script, the next skill to build is navigating input data precisely. DataWeave offers a family of selectors that let you drill into objects and arrays, reach XML attributes, and gracefully handle missing data without throwing errors. Getting comfortable with these selectors is the single biggest productivity boost when working with DataWeave.

Single Value Selector

The dot operator . retrieves the value of a named key from an object. It is the selector you will use most often.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  name: payload.customer.name,
  city: payload.customer.address.city
}

Multi-Value Selector

The double dot operator .. collects every value matching a key name at any depth, returning an array. This is useful for XML documents where a key might repeat inside different parent elements.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload..price

Index and Range Selectors

Square brackets select elements from an array by position. A single index like [0] returns one element; a range like [0 to 2] returns a sub-array; a negative index like [-1] counts from the end.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  first: payload.items[0],
  lastTwo: payload.items[-2 to -1],
  firstThree: payload.items[0 to 2]
}

Attribute Selector

When working with XML, element attributes are reached with .@. This returns an object of all attributes, or you can chain a key to get a single one, such as payload.order.@id.

%dw 2.0
input payload application/xml
output application/json
---
{
  orderId: payload.order.@id,
  allAttributes: payload.order.@
}

Optional and Default-Safe Selectors

Selecting a key that does not exist normally returns null rather than throwing an error, which makes DataWeave forgiving by default. To supply a fallback value, combine a selector with the default keyword. To check existence without triggering type coercion errors, use the ? operator after a selector.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  discount: payload.discount default 0,
  hasCoupon: payload.coupon?
}

Selector Reference

SelectorSyntaxPurpose
Single value.Get one key's value
Multi value..Get all matches at any depth as an array
Index[n]Get array element at position n
Range[n to m]Get a slice of an array
Attribute.@nameGet an XML attribute value
Existence check?Returns boolean whether the selector resolved
Note: The multi-value selector .. always returns an array, even if only one match exists, which is a common source of confusion when chaining further selectors after it.

Dynamic Key Selection

Sometimes the key you need to select is not known until runtime — for example, it might come from a variable or from another part of the payload. DataWeave supports this with the bracket-and-parentheses form obj[(keyExpression)], which evaluates the inner expression to determine which key to read.

%dw 2.0
var fieldName = "customer"
output application/json
---
{
  dynamicField: payload[(fieldName)],
  allKeys: keysOf(payload)
}

This pattern is especially useful in generic mapping utilities where field names are supplied through a configuration object rather than hardcoded directly into the script, keeping transformation logic reusable across similar but not identical payloads.

Key Points

  • Use . for direct key access and .. to gather matches from nested structures.
  • Array elements are accessed with [index] or sliced with [start to end], including negative indices.
  • XML attributes require the @ selector, separate from element content.
  • Combine selectors with default to avoid null values propagating into your output.

subtopics.title: DataWeave Data Types
subtopics.meta_description: Explore DataWeave 2.0's rich type system, including String, Number, Boolean, Array, Object, and Date/Time types, plus type coercion using the as operator.
subtopics.summary: DataWeave has a rich, native type system that goes well beyond JSON's basic types, including dedicated date, time, and range types.
subtopics.content_html:
DataWeave is a typed language even though it feels lightweight to write. Every value that flows through a script belongs to one of DataWeave's built-in types, and understanding these types is essential for writing predictable transformations, especially when converting between formats that model data differently, such as XML (which is text-based) and JSON (which has native numbers and booleans).

Core Types

TypeExample LiteralNotes
String"hello"Double or single quotes accepted
Number42, 3.14No separate int/float; arbitrary precision
Booleantrue, false 
NullnullAbsence of a value
Array[1, 2, 3]Ordered, heterogeneous
Object{ a: 1, b: 2 }Ordered key-value pairs; keys may repeat
Binaryfrom a streamRaw bytes, e.g. file contents
Range1 to 5Lazily enumerable sequence of numbers
Function(x) -> x * 2First-class values

Date and Time Types

DataWeave separates temporal values into distinct types rather than using a single generic "date" concept: Date, Time, DateTime, LocalDateTime, LocalTime, Period, and TimeZone. This precision avoids the ambiguity of comparing a date-only value with a full timestamp.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  today: now() as Date,
  isoTimestamp: now() as String {format: "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss"},
  fromString: "2026-08-20" as Date,
  addFiveDays: ("2026-08-20" as Date) + |P5D|
}

Type Coercion with as

The as operator explicitly converts a value from one type to another, optionally with formatting options in curly braces called a schema. This is the mechanism used constantly when parsing incoming strings into numbers or dates, or serializing numbers back into formatted strings.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  price: payload.priceText as Number,
  formattedPrice: (payload.priceText as Number) as String {format: "#,##0.00"},
  quantity: payload.qty as Number {format: "#"}
}

Checking Types at Runtime

The typeOf() function and the is keyword let a script branch based on a value's runtime type, which is especially handy in pattern matching or when input data is inconsistently typed.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (item) -> {
  value: item,
  type: typeOf(item),
  isNumeric: item is Number
}
Tip: The Nothing type represents a computation that legitimately has no value, distinct from Null, and is mostly seen internally in DataWeave's own type signatures.

Defining Custom Types

The type keyword lets a script or module declare a named alias for a shape, which improves readability and can be reused across function signatures. Custom types can also add constraints, such as restricting a String to particular literal values, effectively creating a simple enumeration.

%dw 2.0
type OrderStatus = "PENDING" | "SHIPPED" | "DELIVERED" | "CANCELLED"
type Order = {
  id: Number,
  status: OrderStatus,
  total: Number
}
output application/json
---
payload.orders map (o) -> o as Order

Key Points

  • DataWeave has a single Number type covering both integers and decimals with arbitrary precision.
  • Dedicated Date, Time, DateTime, and Period types make temporal arithmetic and formatting explicit and safe.
  • The as operator performs type coercion and accepts a formatting schema in curly braces.
  • Objects in DataWeave are ordered and can contain duplicate keys, unlike a standard Java Map.

subtopics.title: DataWeave Functions
subtopics.meta_description: Learn to use DataWeave 2.0's built-in functions such as map, filter, reduce, and pluck, plus how to write your own reusable custom fun declarations in scripts.
subtopics.summary: DataWeave ships dozens of built-in higher-order functions for arrays and objects, and also lets you define reusable custom functions.
subtopics.content_html:
Functions are the workhorses of DataWeave. Because DataWeave is a functional language, transformations are typically expressed by composing small functions rather than writing imperative loops. The core module, dw::core::Arrays, and related modules are imported automatically, so functions like map, filter, and reduce are always available without an explicit import.

map, filter, and reduce

map transforms every element of an array into a new value, filter keeps only elements matching a condition, and reduce collapses an array into a single accumulated value.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  activeNames: payload.users filter (u) -> u.status == "ACTIVE" map (u) -> u.name,
  totalAge: payload.users.age reduce (age, total = 0) -> total + age
}

pluck and other Array helpers

pluck extracts one part of every key-value pair in an object, returning an array. Other frequently used array functions include sizeOf, distinctBy, orderBy, groupBy, flatten, and joinBy.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  fieldNames: payload pluck $$,
  fieldValues: payload pluck $,
  sortedByPrice: payload.items orderBy $.price,
  grouped: payload.items groupBy $.category
}

Inside these expressions, $ refers to the current value and $$ refers to the current key or index — a shorthand that avoids naming a parameter explicitly for short lambdas.

Writing Custom Functions

Use the fun keyword to declare a named, reusable function in the header of a script or inside a module. Functions can take default parameter values and can be recursive.

%dw 2.0
output application/json

fun applyTax(amount: Number, rate: Number = 0.08): Number =
  amount + (amount * rate)

fun factorial(n: Number): Number =
  if (n <= 1) 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)
---
{
  taxedTotal: applyTax(payload.subtotal),
  taxedCustomRate: applyTax(payload.subtotal, 0.15),
  itemFactorial: factorial(5)
}

Anonymous Functions (Lambdas)

Functions are values in DataWeave, so they can be assigned to variables or passed as arguments using arrow syntax.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var double = (x: Number) -> x * 2
---
payload.numbers map double

Commonly Used Built-In Functions

FunctionModulePurpose
map / mapObjectcoreTransform array elements or object entries
filtercoreKeep elements matching a condition
reducecoreAccumulate a single result from an array
pluckcoreExtract keys or values from an object
sizeOfcoreCount elements/characters
upper / lowerdw::core::StringsChange string case
Tip: Prefer chaining built-in functions like filter and map over writing manual recursive loops — they are more readable and the DataWeave engine optimizes them well.

Key Points

  • map, filter, and reduce cover the majority of array transformation needs.
  • $ and $$ are shorthand references to the current value and key/index inside lambdas.
  • Custom functions are declared with fun and support typed parameters with default values.
  • Functions are first-class values that can be stored in variables and passed around like any other type.

subtopics.title: DataWeave Array Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 array function reference covering map, filter, reduce, flatMap, pluck, orderBy, groupBy, distinctBy and more, with fully worked examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of the most commonly used DataWeave 2.0 array functions, each explained with a worked input-to-output example.
subtopics.content_html:
Arrays are the data shape you touch most often in integration work — lists of orders, records from a database query, rows from a CSV. DataWeave's core module ships a rich set of array functions that cover mapping, filtering, aggregating and reshaping without ever needing a manual loop. This page collects the ones you will reach for constantly, each with a short description and a working example.

FunctionDescriptionExample
mapTransforms each element, producing a new array of the same length[1,2,3] map ($ * 2) → [2,4,6]
filterKeeps only elements matching a condition[1,2,3,4] filter ($ mod 2 == 0) → [2,4]
reduceFolds an array down to a single accumulated value[1,2,3] reduce ((item, acc=0) -> acc + item) → 6
flatMapMaps then flattens one level of nested arrays[[1,2],[3]] flatMap ($ map $ * 10) → [10,20,30]
pluckExtracts key, value or index triples (also works on arrays of objects)payload pluck .price
orderBySorts elements by a derived key, ascending by defaultpayload orderBy $.age
groupByBuckets elements into an object keyed by a derived valuepayload groupBy $.status
distinctByRemoves duplicate elements based on a derived keypayload distinctBy $.email
joinByJoins array elements into a single string with a separator["a","b","c"] joinBy "-" → "a-b-c"
sizeOfReturns the number of elements in an arraysizeOf [1,2,3] → 3
flattenCollapses nested arrays into a single flat arrayflatten [[1,2],[3,[4]]] → [1,2,3,[4]]
zip / unzipPairs up elements from parallel arrays, or reverses that pairing[1,2] zip ["a","b"] → [[1,"a"],[2,"b"]]
some / everyTests whether any or all elements satisfy a condition[1,2,3] every ($ > 0) → true
splitBySplits an array (or string) into chunks around a matcher[1,2,0,3] splitBy ($ == 0)

Example 1: Shaping an Order List

A typical integration step takes a raw array of order records, filters out cancelled ones, and reshapes each surviving record.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "COMPLETE", total: 42.50 },
  { id: 2, status: "CANCELLED", total: 10.00 },
  { id: 3, status: "COMPLETE", total: 99.90 }
]
---
orders
  filter ($.status == "COMPLETE")
  map (o) -> { orderId: o.id, amountDue: o.total }

/* Output:
[
  { "orderId": 1, "amountDue": 42.5 },
  { "orderId": 3, "amountDue": 99.9 }
]
*/

Example 2: Aggregating Totals with reduce

reduce is the general-purpose tool for turning an array into a single value, such as a running total or a concatenated string.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var totals = [42.50, 10.00, 99.90]
---
{
  grandTotal: totals reduce ((amount, acc=0) -> acc + amount)
}

/* Output:
{ "grandTotal": 152.4 }
*/

Example 3: Grouping and Deduplicating

groupBy and distinctBy both take a key-selector lambda and are frequently combined with pluck or map immediately afterward to reshape the resulting buckets.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var customers = [
  { id: 1, region: "EMEA" },
  { id: 2, region: "APAC" },
  { id: 3, region: "EMEA" }
]
---
customers groupBy $.region

/* Output:
{
  "EMEA": [ { "id": 1, "region": "EMEA" }, { "id": 3, "region": "EMEA" } ],
  "APAC": [ { "id": 2, "region": "APAC" } ]
}
*/

Key Points

  • map and filter are the two functions you will reach for the most; both preserve or shrink the array without changing its overall shape.
  • reduce is the escape hatch for any aggregation that isn't already a built-in function — sums, string joins, custom accumulators.
  • groupBy and orderBy both take a key-selector, not a full comparator, which keeps common cases concise.
  • flatten only removes one level of nesting per call; nest calls or use flatMap for deeper structures.
  • Most array functions are non-mutating — they always return a new array, leaving the original untouched.

Chaining Array Functions

DataWeave's pipeline-friendly syntax makes it natural to chain several array functions in sequence, reading top to bottom as a series of steps rather than nested calls. A common pattern is filter, then map, then orderBy, which mirrors how you would describe the transformation in plain English: take the completed orders, extract just the fields needed, and sort them by date. Because each function returns a new array, chaining does not require intermediate variables, though naming an intermediate step with a var can still help readability in longer pipelines.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "COMPLETE", placedOn: |2026-08-01|, total: 42.50 },
  { id: 2, status: "CANCELLED", placedOn: |2026-08-05|, total: 10.00 },
  { id: 3, status: "COMPLETE", placedOn: |2026-07-15|, total: 99.90 }
]
---
orders
  filter ($.status == "COMPLETE")
  map (o) -> { orderId: o.id, placedOn: o.placedOn, total: o.total }
  orderBy $.placedOn

/* Output:
[
  { "orderId": 3, "placedOn": "2026-07-15", "total": 99.9 },
  { "orderId": 1, "placedOn": "2026-08-01", "total": 42.5 }
]
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Object Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 object function reference covering mapObject, pluck, entrySet, valuesOf, namesOf, mergeWith and filterObject, with fully worked examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of the DataWeave 2.0 functions used to transform, inspect and merge object structures, illustrated with worked examples.
subtopics.content_html:
Objects in DataWeave are ordered collections of key-value pairs, and unlike many languages, keys are not required to be unique — a fact that shapes how several of these functions behave. This reference covers the functions you need to reshape objects, inspect their keys and values, and merge two objects together.

FunctionDescriptionExample
mapObjectTransforms each key-value pair, returning a new object{a:1,b:2} mapObject (v,k) -> { (k): v * 10 }
pluckExtracts keys, values, or indices from an object into arrays{a:1,b:2} pluck $ → [1,2]
entrySet / entriesOfReturns an array of {key, value} entry objectsentriesOf({a:1}) → [{key:"a",value:1}]
valuesOfReturns just the values of an object as an arrayvaluesOf({a:1,b:2}) → [1,2]
namesOf / keysOfReturns just the key names of an object as an arraynamesOf({a:1,b:2}) → ["a","b"]
mergeWithMerges two objects, with the right-hand object's keys winning on conflicts{a:1,b:2} mergeWith {b:99} → {a:1,b:99}
filterObjectKeeps only key-value pairs matching a condition{a:1,b:2} filterObject (v,k) -> v > 1

Example 1: Renaming and Recomputing Values with mapObject

mapObject is the object counterpart to map: the lambda receives value, key (and optionally index), and returns a single-entry object that gets merged into the result — which is also how you rename keys on the fly.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var prices = { widgetPrice: 10, gadgetPrice: 25 }
---
prices mapObject (value, key) -> {
  (key replace "Price" with "PriceWithTax"): value * 1.2
}

/* Output:
{ "widgetPriceWithTax": 12, "gadgetPriceWithTax": 30 }
*/

Example 2: Inspecting an Object's Shape

namesOf, valuesOf and entriesOf are handy whenever you need to treat an object generically — for example, building a summary of an unknown payload's fields.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var record = { id: 7, name: "Ada", active: true }
---
{
  fieldNames: namesOf(record),
  fieldCount: sizeOf(namesOf(record)),
  entries: entriesOf(record)
}

/* Output:
{
  "fieldNames": ["id", "name", "active"],
  "fieldCount": 3,
  "entries": [
    { "key": "id", "value": 7 },
    { "key": "name", "value": "Ada" },
    { "key": "active", "value": true }
  ]
}
*/

Example 3: Merging Defaults with Overrides

mergeWith is a clean way to layer a set of overrides on top of a defaults object without writing manual conditional logic, and filterObject can trim the result afterward.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var defaults = { retries: 3, timeoutMs: 5000, debug: false }
var overrides = { timeoutMs: 8000, debug: true }
---
(defaults mergeWith overrides) filterObject (value, key) -> value != false

/* Output:
{ "retries": 3, "timeoutMs": 8000, "debug": true }
*/

Key Points

  • mapObject lets you change keys, values, or both in a single pass, since the lambda returns a whole key-value pair.
  • pluck and valuesOf/namesOf both extract data from objects but pluck can target keys, values or indices depending on the selector used.
  • mergeWith is right-biased: the argument object's keys overwrite the caller's on conflicts.
  • Because DataWeave objects can hold duplicate keys, functions like entriesOf preserve every entry rather than collapsing to a map.
  • filterObject mirrors filter for arrays, but its lambda receives both the value and the key.

A Note on Duplicate Keys

DataWeave objects are ordered sequences of key-value pairs rather than strict maps, so two entries can legally share the same key. This matters for functions like valuesOf and entriesOf, which will faithfully return every entry, duplicates included, whereas a naive property lookup such as obj.key only ever returns the first matching value. When a source system emits repeated keys (a common quirk of XML converted to DataWeave objects, where repeated child elements become repeated keys) use obj.*key to select every value for that key as an array, rather than relying on the single-value selector.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var xmlLike = { item: "Widget", item: "Gadget", item: "Gizmo" }
---
{
  firstOnly: xmlLike.item,
  allValues: xmlLike.*item,
  count: sizeOf(xmlLike.*item)
}

/* Output:
{
  "firstOnly": "Widget",
  "allValues": ["Widget", "Gadget", "Gizmo"],
  "count": 3
}
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave String Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 string function reference covering upper, lower, trim, splitBy, contains, camelize, replace, matches, leftPad and more, with examples.
subtopics.summary: A reference of frequently used DataWeave 2.0 string functions for casing, trimming, splitting, matching and padding text values.
subtopics.content_html:
String manipulation shows up constantly in integration flows: normalizing case before a comparison, cleaning up whitespace from a legacy system, validating a format with a regular expression, or padding an identifier to a fixed width for a fixed-length flat file. DataWeave's string functions cover all of these without reaching for a scripting language.

FunctionDescriptionExample
upper / lowerConverts a string to upper or lower caseupper("abc") → "ABC"
trimRemoves leading and trailing whitespacetrim(" hi ") → "hi"
splitBySplits a string into an array around a matcher"a,b,c" splitBy "," → ["a","b","c"]
joinByJoins an array of strings back into one string["a","b"] joinBy "-" → "a-b"
containsTests whether a string contains a substring"hello" contains "ell" → true
startsWith / endsWithTests the beginning or end of a string"invoice.pdf" endsWith ".pdf" → true
camelizeConverts snake_case or kebab-case to camelCasecamelize("order_id") → "orderId"
replaceReplaces matched text with a replacement"2026-08-20" replace "-" with "/"
matchesTests a string against a regular expression"abc123" matches /^[a-z]+[0-9]+$/ → true
leftPad / rightPadPads a string to a fixed length"7" leftPad 4 with "0" → "0007"
substringExtracts a portion of a string by index"hello world" [0 to 4] → "hello"

Example 1: Normalizing Incoming Field Names

Legacy systems frequently emit snake_case or ALL CAPS field names. Combining lower, camelize and trim is a common first step before mapping fields into a clean canonical model.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var raw = { "CUSTOMER_ID ": 501, " first_name": "Ada " }
---
raw mapObject (value, key) -> {
  (camelize(trim(lower(key)))): if (value is String) trim(value) else value
}

/* Output:
{ "customerId": 501, "firstName": "Ada" }
*/

Example 2: Validating and Reformatting an Identifier

matches is useful for guarding a transformation with a validation check, while leftPad normalizes width for downstream systems that expect fixed-length codes.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var skus = ["7", "842", "15"]
---
skus map (sku) -> {
  original: sku,
  isNumeric: sku matches /^[0-9]+$/,
  padded: sku leftPad 5 with "0"
}

/* Output:
[
  { "original": "7", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00007" },
  { "original": "842", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00842" },
  { "original": "15", "isNumeric": true, "padded": "00015" }
]
*/

Example 3: Splitting and Rejoining a Delimited Value

splitBy and joinBy are frequently paired when reformatting a delimited value, such as converting a comma-separated tag list into a pipe-separated one after trimming each entry.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var tagString = "urgent, billing , escalated"
---
(tagString splitBy ",") map (t) -> trim(t) joinBy " | "

/* Output:
"urgent | billing | escalated"
*/

Key Points

  • upper, lower, trim and camelize are commonly chained together when normalizing field names or values from legacy sources.
  • splitBy and joinBy work as an inverse pair for delimited strings, similar to their array counterparts.
  • matches takes a regular expression literal (/pattern/), not a string, and returns a boolean.
  • leftPad/rightPad are essential when producing fixed-width output for flat files or legacy record formats.
  • Most string functions are case- and locale-sensitive; use upper/lower explicitly before comparisons when case should not matter.

Chaining String Transformations Safely

String functions compose cleanly, but real payloads are rarely as clean as the examples above — a field might be null, or a number might arrive typed as a String. Wrapping a chain of string functions with a null check (or a default fallback) avoids runtime errors when a field is missing entirely, and casting explicitly with as String avoids type-mismatch errors when the underlying value is not already text.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var records = [
  { code: "  ab-12 " },
  { code: null },
  { code: 4500 }
]
---
records map (r) -> {
  cleaned: upper(trim(r.code default "" as String))
}

/* Output:
[
  { "cleaned": "AB-12" },
  { "cleaned": "" },
  { "cleaned": "4500" }
]
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Date, Time and Number Functions Reference
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 reference for date and time handling with now, the | operator, daysBetween, date arithmetic and number functions like round and random.
subtopics.summary: A reference of DataWeave 2.0 functions and operators for working with dates, times and numbers, shown with worked examples.
subtopics.content_html:
Dates and numbers each have their own quirks in any transformation language, and DataWeave provides a focused set of functions and operators to handle both: converting between string formats, measuring elapsed time, and rounding or randomizing numeric values. This page covers the ones you will use most in day-to-day integration work.

Function / OperatorDescriptionExample
now()Returns the current DateTime including timezonenow() → 2026-08-20T14:03:00Z
asCasts/parses or formats a value using a target type and format"2026-08-20" as Date {format: "yyyy-MM-dd"}
| (format operator)Formats a Date/DateTime/Time value using a pattern stringnow() as String {format: "dd/MM/yyyy"}
daysBetweenReturns whole days between two datesdaysBetween(\|2026-01-01\|, \|2026-01-11\|) → 10
+ / - on PeriodAdds or subtracts a Period from a date/time value\|2026-01-01\| + \|P7D\|
roundRounds a number to the nearest integerround(4.6) → 5
ceil / floorRounds up or down to the nearest integerceil(4.1) → 5, floor(4.9) → 4
random()Returns a pseudo-random Number between 0 and 1random()
isDecimalTests whether a Number has a non-zero decimal partisDecimal(4.5) → true

Example 1: Formatting a Timestamp for an Outbound API

Incoming and outgoing systems rarely agree on date format. DataWeave's date literals (\|value\|) combined with the as operator handle both parsing and formatting.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var orderPlaced = |2026-08-20T09:15:00Z|
---
{
  isoTimestamp: orderPlaced as String,
  displayDate: orderPlaced as String {format: "MMM d, yyyy"},
  compactDate: orderPlaced as String {format: "yyyyMMdd"}
}

/* Output:
{
  "isoTimestamp": "2026-08-20T09:15:00Z",
  "displayDate": "Aug 20, 2026",
  "compactDate": "20260820"
}
*/

Example 2: Calculating SLA Age with daysBetween

Comparing two dates to compute an elapsed duration is a common requirement for SLA and aging reports.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var ticket = { opened: |2026-08-01|, dueInDays: 14 }
var today = |2026-08-20|
---
{
  ageInDays: daysBetween(ticket.opened, today),
  dueDate: ticket.opened + |P14D|,
  isOverdue: daysBetween(ticket.opened, today) > ticket.dueInDays
}

/* Output:
{
  "ageInDays": 19,
  "dueDate": "2026-08-15",
  "isOverdue": true
}
*/

Example 3: Rounding Prices and Flagging Fractional Quantities

Number functions like round, ceil, floor and isDecimal are common in pricing and inventory calculations where fractional units need special handling.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var lines = [
  { sku: "A1", qty: 3.5, unitPrice: 9.995 },
  { sku: "B2", qty: 2, unitPrice: 14.499 }
]
---
lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  roundedPrice: round(line.unitPrice * 100) / 100,
  wholeUnitsNeeded: ceil(line.qty),
  hasPartialQuantity: isDecimal(line.qty)
}

/* Output:
[
  { "sku": "A1", "roundedPrice": 10.0, "wholeUnitsNeeded": 4, "hasPartialQuantity": true },
  { "sku": "B2", "roundedPrice": 14.5, "wholeUnitsNeeded": 2, "hasPartialQuantity": false }
]
*/

Key Points

  • Date, Time and DateTime literals are written between pipes, like \|2026-08-20\|, and are distinct types from strings.
  • The as operator handles both parsing a string into a date type and formatting a date type back into a string, driven by the format option.
  • daysBetween and Period arithmetic (+/- with \|P...\| literals) cover the majority of duration calculations without manual math.
  • round, ceil and floor all return integers but differ in rounding direction, which matters for billing and inventory logic.
  • isDecimal is a quick guard for distinguishing whole quantities from fractional ones before applying business rules.

Working Across Time Zones

DateTime literals carry a timezone offset, and DataWeave preserves it through arithmetic rather than silently normalizing to UTC. When comparing or displaying timestamps from systems in different zones, convert explicitly rather than assuming two DateTime values are already aligned. The as operator combined with a {format: ...} option and a timezone-aware pattern lets you render the same instant in a specific zone for display, while comparisons and duration math continue to operate on the underlying instant correctly regardless of the zone each value was written in.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var meetingUtc = |2026-08-20T18:00:00Z|
var submittedLocal = |2026-08-20T14:00:00-04:00|
---
{
  sameInstant: meetingUtc == submittedLocal,
  utcDisplay: meetingUtc as String {format: "HH:mm 'UTC'"},
  localZoneDisplay: submittedLocal as String {format: "HH:mm xxx"}
}

/* Output:
{
  "sameInstant": true,
  "utcDisplay": "18:00 UTC",
  "localZoneDisplay": "14:00 -04:00"
}
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Core Module Functions (read, write, flatten and more)
subtopics.meta_description: A DataWeave 2.0 reference for core module functions including read, write, flatten, mapObject vs map, typeOf, isEmpty, sizeOf and the default operator.
subtopics.summary: A reference of foundational DataWeave 2.0 core module functions used for dynamic parsing, serialization, type inspection and null-safe defaults.
subtopics.content_html:
Beyond the array, object and string helpers, DataWeave's core module includes a handful of foundational functions that show up in almost every non-trivial transform: dynamically parsing and serializing data, inspecting a value's runtime type, checking for emptiness, and safely falling back to a default when a value is missing.

Function / OperatorDescriptionExample
read()Parses a string (or binary) into structured data using a given MIME typeread(payload, "application/json")
write()Serializes structured data into a string using a given MIME typewrite(payload, "application/xml")
flattenCollapses one level of nested arrays into a single arrayflatten [[1,2],[3]] → [1,2,3]
mapObject vs mapmap iterates arrays; mapObject iterates key-value pairs of objectssee comparison below
typeOfReturns the runtime type of a valuetypeOf(1) → Number
isEmptyTests whether a string, array or object has no contentisEmpty([]) → true
sizeOfReturns length/count for strings, arrays and objectssizeOf("abc") → 3
defaultSubstitutes a fallback value when the left side is nullpayload.discount default 0

Example 1: Parsing an Embedded JSON String with read()

APIs sometimes embed a JSON or XML document as a plain string field. read() parses that string on demand so you can navigate it just like any other structured value.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var event = {
  eventId: "evt-1",
  payloadJson: "{\"orderId\": 88, \"total\": 120.5}"
}
---
{
  eventId: event.eventId,
  orderId: read(event.payloadJson, "application/json").orderId,
  total: read(event.payloadJson, "application/json").total
}

/* Output:
{ "eventId": "evt-1", "orderId": 88, "total": 120.5 }
*/

Example 2: Serializing to XML with write()

write() is the inverse of read(): it takes structured data and produces a string in the target format, which is useful when you need a formatted string mid-flow rather than relying on the transform's output directive alone.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var order = { id: 1, item: "Widget", qty: 3 }
---
{
  orderId: order.id,
  xmlSnippet: write(order, "application/xml", { writeDeclaration: false })
}

/* Output (xmlSnippet is a string containing):
{
  "orderId": 1,
  "xmlSnippet": "<order><id>1</id><item>Widget</item><qty>3</qty></order>"
}
*/

Example 3: Defensive Defaults, Emptiness and Type Checks

The default operator, isEmpty and typeOf are commonly combined to write transforms that tolerate missing or oddly-shaped upstream data without throwing errors.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var customer = { name: "Ada", tags: [], discountCode: null }
---
{
  name: customer.name default "Unknown",
  hasTags: !isEmpty(customer.tags),
  discountCode: customer.discountCode default "NONE",
  nameType: typeOf(customer.name)
}

/* Output:
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "hasTags": false,
  "discountCode": "NONE",
  "nameType": "String"
}
*/

mapObject vs. map: Choosing the Right Iterator

map iterates an array, calling the lambda with each element (and optional index), and always returns an array. mapObject iterates an object's key-value pairs, calling the lambda with value, key (and optional index), and always returns an object, since the lambda must return a single-entry object for each pair. Reaching for the wrong one is a common source of type errors for developers new to DataWeave — if you are iterating payload.items (an array of orders) you want map; if you are iterating the fields of one order object itself, you want mapObject.

Key Points

  • read() and write() let you parse or serialize data dynamically mid-transform, independent of the script's top-level output directive.
  • flatten only removes one level of array nesting per call; deeply nested arrays need repeated or recursive flattening.
  • map operates on arrays and returns arrays; mapObject operates on objects and returns objects — they are not interchangeable.
  • default only kicks in for null, not for empty strings or empty arrays, so pair it with isEmpty checks when those also need a fallback.
  • typeOf and sizeOf are useful defensive tools when a transform must handle payloads whose shape is not fully guaranteed.

sizeOf Across Different Types

sizeOf is polymorphic: on a String it returns character count, on an Array it returns element count, and on an Object it returns the number of key-value pairs (counting duplicate keys separately). This single function replaces the need for type-specific length checks in most validation logic, though it is worth remembering that it throws an error if called on a type that has no defined notion of size, such as a Number or Boolean, so guard with typeOf first when the input's shape is not already known.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
var samples = ["hello", [1,2,3,4], { a: 1, b: 2 }]
---
samples map (s) -> {
  type: typeOf(s),
  size: sizeOf(s)
}

/* Output:
[
  { "type": "String", "size": 5 },
  { "type": "Array", "size": 4 },
  { "type": "Object", "size": 2 }
]
*/

subtopics.title: DataWeave Modules
subtopics.meta_description: Understand DataWeave 2.0's built-in modules such as dw::core::Strings and dw::core::Arrays, plus how to import and build your own custom reusable modules.
subtopics.summary: Modules organize DataWeave's standard library and also let teams package their own reusable functions and types for import.
subtopics.content_html:
As transformation logic grows across a project, copying the same helper function into every Transform Message component becomes unmanageable. DataWeave solves this with modules: namespaced collections of functions, variables, and types that can be imported wherever they are needed, both from the standard library and from your own project.

The Standard Library Modules

DataWeave's core functions such as map, filter, and arithmetic operators are always available without an import. Many additional functions, however, live in named modules that must be imported explicitly with the import directive.

ModuleContains
dw::core::Stringscamelize, capitalize, splitBy, trim, isBlank, dasherize
dw::core::Arrayssum, avg, countBy, splitWhere, partition, drop, take
dw::core::ObjectsentrySet, mergeWith, nameSet, valueSet, takeWhile
dw::core::NumbersfromBinary, fromHex, toRadixNumber
dw::core::URLencodeURIComponent, decodeURIComponent
dw::Runtimewait, Try, fail — useful for error simulation and control
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Strings
import avg, sum from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
{
  slug: camelize(payload.title),
  isEmpty: isBlank(payload.notes),
  averagePrice: avg(payload.items.price),
  totalPrice: sum(payload.items.price)
}

Building a Custom Module

A custom module is simply a .dwl file placed under src/main/resources (commonly inside a subfolder such as modules) containing only a header of fun, var, or type declarations — no --- body expression is required.

%dw 2.0

type Money = Number

fun formatCurrency(amount: Money, currency: String = "USD"): String =
  currency ++ " " ++ (amount as String {format: "#,##0.00"})

fun applyDiscount(amount: Money, pct: Number): Money =
  amount - (amount * (pct / 100))

Save the file as modules/Pricing.dwl. Any Transform Message or .dwl file in the project can then import it by its relative module path.

%dw 2.0
import * from modules::Pricing
output application/json
---
payload.orders map (order) -> {
  id: order.id,
  finalPrice: formatCurrency(applyDiscount(order.amount, 10))
}
Note: Module names in the import statement use double-colon path separators that mirror the folder structure under src/main/resources, not the file system slash.

Why Teams Adopt Custom Modules

On larger integration projects, the same business rules — currency formatting, address normalization, discount calculations, ID generation — tend to appear in multiple APIs. Without modules, developers either copy-paste DataWeave snippets between projects (which drifts out of sync over time) or drop into Java classes for anything reusable, losing the conciseness DataWeave offers. Packaging shared logic as a module keeps it in one place, testable, and versioned alongside the rest of the project.

Modules can also declare shared type definitions, which is valuable for keeping request and response shapes consistent across every flow that produces or consumes a particular kind of record, such as a canonical Customer or Order type used throughout an API-led architecture.

Key Points

  • Standard library modules like dw::core::Strings must be explicitly imported to use their functions.
  • Custom modules are plain .dwl files containing only declarations, with no body expression.
  • Modules promote reuse of pricing rules, formatting logic, and validation across many flows.
  • Use import * from module to bring in everything, or list specific names to import selectively.

subtopics.title: Transforming JSON, XML and CSV
subtopics.meta_description: Learn practical DataWeave 2.0 techniques for converting between JSON, XML, and CSV formats, including namespaces, attributes, and CSV header settings.
subtopics.summary: Converting between JSON, XML, and CSV is one of the most common integration tasks, and DataWeave handles each format's quirks with dedicated directives.
subtopics.content_html:
Integration flows constantly move data between systems that speak different formats: a REST API returning JSON, a legacy SOAP service expecting XML, and a nightly batch file in CSV. DataWeave reads and writes all three natively, but each format has structural quirks worth understanding before you write conversion logic.

XML to JSON

XML documents are inherently hierarchical and attribute-aware, while JSON has no concept of attributes and represents repeated elements as arrays rather than repeated keys. When converting XML to JSON, use the multi-value or key selector carefully, and wrap single repeating elements in an array explicitly if the source might contain only one occurrence.

%dw 2.0
input payload application/xml
output application/json
---
{
  orderId: payload.order.@id,
  customer: payload.order.customer,
  items: payload.order.items.*item map (i) -> {
    sku: i.sku,
    qty: i.qty as Number,
    price: i.price as Number
  }
}

The *item selector explicitly selects every item element as an array, which avoids the common bug where a document with only one <item> element accidentally produces an object instead of a single-element array.

JSON to XML

Going the other direction, DataWeave needs an explicit root element because JSON does not require one but XML always does. Attributes are written using the @ key inside an object.

%dw 2.0
output application/xml
---
order @(id: payload.orderId as String): {
  customer: payload.customer,
  items: {
    item: payload.items map (i) -> {
      sku: i.sku,
      qty: i.qty,
      price: i.price
    }
  }
}

Working with CSV

CSV is flat and always tabular, so nested JSON structures generally need to be flattened before writing CSV, and CSV rows always arrive as an array of objects when read. Common output directive options include header, separator, and quoteValues.

%dw 2.0
output application/csv separator=",", quoteValues=true, header=true
---
payload.orders map (order) -> {
  orderId: order.id,
  customerName: order.customer.name,
  total: order.items reduce (item, acc = 0) -> acc + (item.price * item.qty)
}

Reading CSV with Custom Delimiters

%dw 2.0
input payload application/csv separator=";", header=true
output application/json
---
payload map (row) -> {
  id: row.ID as Number,
  name: row.NAME
}

Format Directive Cheat Sheet

MIME TypeCommon Options
application/jsonindent (pretty-print toggle)
application/xmlwriteDeclaration, namespaces via ns
application/csvheader, separator, quoteValues, lineSeparator
Tip: When XML namespaces are involved, declare them with the ns directive in the header (for example ns soap http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/) so selectors and output construction can reference the correct prefix.

Converting Between JSON and CSV

Since both formats are relatively simple compared to XML, JSON-to-CSV and CSV-to-JSON conversions are usually the most straightforward, provided the JSON payload is already an array of flat objects. If the source JSON is nested, flatten it first in the same script with a map that pulls nested fields up to the top level before the output directive serializes the array as CSV rows.

Key Points

  • XML requires a single root element; JSON does not, so JSON-to-XML transforms must supply one explicitly.
  • Use *element to force a consistent array shape when converting repeatable XML elements to JSON.
  • CSV output is controlled with directive options like header, separator, and quoteValues.
  • Flatten nested structures before writing CSV, since CSV cannot represent nested objects.

subtopics.title: DataWeave Operators and Pattern Matching
subtopics.meta_description: Review DataWeave 2.0's operators for arithmetic, comparison, and logic, and learn the match expression for type-based and structural pattern matching.
subtopics.summary: DataWeave provides a full operator set plus a match expression that branches logic based on a value's type, shape, or content.
subtopics.content_html:
Beyond selectors and functions, DataWeave scripts frequently need to compare, combine, and branch on values. DataWeave's operator set covers arithmetic, string concatenation, and logic, while its match expression provides a concise, declarative alternative to long chains of if/else statements.

Arithmetic and String Operators

OperatorPurposeExample
+ - * /Arithmetic on numbersprice * qty
++Concatenate strings, arrays, or objects"Hello " ++ name
--Remove item(s) from an array or object[1,2,3] -- [2]
updateImmutably update a nested fieldpayload update "price" with 9.99

Comparison and Logical Operators

DataWeave supports the standard comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) along with and, or, and not for boolean logic. The ~= operator performs a type-flexible "similar to" comparison, useful when comparing a string to a number without an explicit cast.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  isExpensive: payload.price > 100,
  isValid: payload.qty >= 1 and payload.price > 0,
  looksEqual: "5" ~= 5,
  strictEqual: "5" == 5
}

The default and orElse Operators

default supplies a fallback when a selector resolves to null or fails. orElse similarly provides a fallback specifically when an expression throws an error, which is more targeted than wrapping code in a full try-style construct.

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  region: payload.region default "UNKNOWN",
  parsedAmount: (payload.amount as Number) orElse 0
}

Pattern Matching with match

The match expression evaluates a value against a series of case clauses, each testing either a type, a literal value, or a structural shape, and falls through to a default or wildcard clause when nothing else matches.

%dw 2.0
output application/json

fun describe(value: Any): String = value match {
  case is Null -> "empty value"
  case n is Number if (n > 100) -> "large number"
  case n is Number -> "small number"
  case s is String -> "text: " ++ s
  case { status: "ACTIVE" } -> "active record"
  case arr is Array -> "array of " ++ (sizeOf(arr) as String) ++ " items"
  else -> "unrecognized"
}
---
payload.samples map describe

Notice the guard clause (if (n > 100)) that adds a condition on top of a type match, and the structural match (case { status: "ACTIVE" }) that checks an object's shape and values directly.

Tip: Order matters in a match expression — DataWeave evaluates cases top to bottom and stops at the first match, so put more specific conditions before general ones.

Key Points

  • The ++ and -- operators concatenate and remove elements across strings, arrays, and objects.
  • default handles null values; orElse handles expressions that throw errors.
  • match supports type checks, literal checks, structural checks, and guard conditions in one construct.
  • Case order in a match expression is significant since the first matching clause wins.
